title: ByteX: A Unified AI Search Engine at ByteDance

    Title:ByteX: A Unified AI Search Engine at ByteDance
View PDF
            Abstract:Since 2016, ByteX has been the foundation of ByteDance's search infrastructure, scaling to more than 7,000 clusters and 300 PB of indexed data. Driven by the demands of AI workloads, ByteX has evolved from a text search engine into a unified AI search system supporting vector retrieval, lexical matching, and predicate filtering. Its largest deployment indexes nearly one trillion high-dimensional vectors. This scale exposes two central bottlenecks in AI-era retrieval: memory-intensive graph-index construction under sustained ingestion, and the prohibitive cost of keeping vector indexes entirely in memory. ByteX addresses these bottlenecks with two techniques. First, it introduces a quantization-aware vector kernel based on SymRaBitQ, a new symmetric quantization scheme with tight theoretical guarantees that allows index construction to run directly in the quantized space accurately and efficiently without retaining a copy of full-precision vectors. Second, it provides a hybrid storage engine that supports memory-resident, hybrid, and SSD-resident deployments, with fine-grained record-level caching to trade memory for latency under operational control. On large-scale benchmarks, ByteX improves throughput by up to 3x, reduces indexing memory by 80%, and lowers operating cost by 86% compared with prior systems, while supporting trillion-vector scale, write-heavy or latency-sensitive workloads in production.

report.summary: ByteDance's ByteX search engine scales to trillions of vectors, using quantization and hybrid storage to cut memory and cost while maintaining performance.
report.background: ByteX has been ByteDance's search engine foundation since 2016, growing to more than 7,000 clusters and 300 PB of indexed data. As AI workloads emerged, ByteX evolved from a pure text search engine into a unified AI search system that supports vector retrieval, lexical matching, and predicate filtering. Its largest deployment holds nearly one trillion high-dimensional vectors. This extreme scale exposed two bottlenecks: memory-intensive graph-index construction under continuous data ingestion, and the prohibitive expense of keeping entire vector indexes in RAM. To address this, ByteX introduces SymRaBitQ, a symmetric quantization scheme with theoretical guarantees that enables index construction directly in quantized space without storing full-precision vectors. It also implements a hybrid storage engine that supports memory-resident, hybrid, and SSD-resident deployments with record-level caching, balancing memory use and latency in production.
key_points: Scale is extreme: ByteX runs on more than 7,000 clusters, manages 300 PB of indexed data, and its largest deployment indexes nearly one trillion high-dimensional vectors. This makes it one of the largest production search and retrieval systems described in public literature.

AI-era retrieval faces two bottlenecks: constructing graph indexes under sustained ingestion consumes enormous memory, and holding vector indexes entirely in RAM is very expensive. ByteX was redesigned to solve these problems rather than simply adding more hardware.

SymRaBitQ is a new quantization-aware vector kernel that allows graph index construction to happen accurately and efficiently in compressed space. It removes the need to keep a copy of full-precision vectors around, dramatically reducing memory pressure during ingestion and indexing.

ByteX introduces a hybrid storage engine that supports memory-resident, hybrid, and SSD-resident modes. Fine-grained record-level caching lets operators trade memory for latency under control, enabling large vector indexes to run cost-effectively without always requiring RAM.

Reported results are strong: throughput improves by up to 3x, indexing memory drops by 80%, and operating cost falls by 86% compared with prior systems. ByteX also handles write-heavy and latency-sensitive workloads in production at trillion-vector scale.
report.impact: ByteX demonstrates that very large AI retrieval systems do not need to keep every vector in memory, which could lower barriers for companies building recommendation engines, semantic search, and RAG pipelines. A hybrid and quantized approach means production systems can support trillion-scale indexes while dramatically reducing hardware costs and ingestion memory. For developers, it suggests practical design patterns: quantized index construction and flexible SSD caching can replace brute-force in-memory assumptions. For regular users, the result is faster, cheaper AI-powered search behind consumer apps. It also raises the competitive bar for vector database vendors, pressuring them to address write-heavy, latency-sensitive, and ultra-large-scale workloads rather than only benchmark-friendly small datasets.
report.tools: ByteX itself is proprietary, but similar ideas can be explored through open-source tools: FAISS for efficient similarity search and quantization, Microsoft DiskANN for SSD-resident vector indexes, Google ScaNN for scalable nearest neighbors, and HNSWLib for graph-based ANN. Managed vector databases like Milvus, Qdrant, and Weaviate also offer disk-based and quantized index options worth experimenting with.
